note: The relationship between the papacy and the Holy Roman Empire oscillated between the cooperative model (Ottonian era: the emperor protects the papacy, the papacy legitimizes the emperor), the catastrophic conflict of the Investiture Controversy (1076–1122), a renewed but unstable cooperation (Crusades), and the existential pope-emperor conflict under Frederick II (1239–1250). The fundamental tension — who holds ultimate authority in Latin Christendom — was never resolved: the papacy's greatest victories (Walk to Canossa 1077, deposition of Frederick II 1245) were matched by imperial resilience; the empire's greatest victories (Synod of Worms 1076, antipopes) were checked by papal ingenuity.

_quarry.structural_significance: The pope-emperor conflict generates medieval Europe's most sophisticated political theory (John of Salisbury, Marsilio of Padua, Thomas Aquinas on secular authority); neither side wins definitively; the conflict's 400-year duration shapes the institutional development of both the papacy and the empire in ways that neither power could have anticipated
